items.text: However, their ability to access and precisely manipulate knowledge is still limited, and hence on knowledge-intensive tasks, their performance lags behind task-speciﬁc architectures.
items.why: States the limitations of current pre-trained language models.
items.plain: Large language models still struggle to access and accurately use factual knowledge, so they perform worse on knowledge-heavy tasks than specialized architectures.

items.text: We explore a general-purpose ﬁne-tuning recipe for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) — models which combine pre-trained parametric and non-parametric memory for language generation.
items.why: Introduces Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for fine-tuning text generation models.
items.plain: We study a general approach to fine-tuning retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) models, which combine stored parameters with an external text index to generate language.

items.text: We ﬁne-tune and evaluate our models on a wide range of knowledgeintensive NLP tasks and set the state of the art on three open domain QA tasks, outperforming parametric seq2seq models and task-speciﬁc retrieve-and-extract architectures.
items.why: Summarizes the overall experimental evaluation and state-of-the-art results.
items.plain: We fine-tune and test our models across many knowledge-heavy language tasks, setting new top scores on three open-domain question answering datasets.

items.text: For language generation tasks, we ﬁnd that RAG models generate more speciﬁc, diverse and factual language than a state-of-the-art parametric-only seq2seq baseline.
items.why: Highlights key generation improvements over baseline models.
items.plain: For text generation, RAG models create more specific, varied, and factual language than standard sequence-to-sequence baselines that lack external retrieval.

items.text: While this development is exciting, such models do have downsides: They cannot easily expand or revise their memory, can’t straightforwardly provide insight into their predictions, and may produce “hallucinations” [38].
items.why: Explains core downsides of relying purely on implicit neural memory.
items.plain: Purely neural models cannot easily update their knowledge, explain their predictions, or prevent false statements.

items.text: Here, we bring hybrid parametric and non-parametric memory to the “workhorse of NLP,” i.e. sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models.
items.why: States the central contribution of adapting hybrid retrieval memory to sequence-to-sequence models.
items.plain: We adapt hybrid memory systems—combining stored network parameters with document retrieval—to standard sequence-to-sequence language models.

items.text: Our RAG models achieve state-of-the-art results on open Natural Questions [29], WebQuestions [3] and CuratedTrec [2] and strongly outperform recent approaches that use specialised pre-training objectives on TriviaQA [24].
items.why: Reports state-of-the-art accuracy gains on specific open-domain QA datasets.
items.plain: Our RAG models set new top results on Natural Questions, WebQuestions, and CuratedTrec, while outperforming customized pre-training approaches on TriviaQA.

items.text: For knowledge-intensive generation, we experiment with MS-MARCO [1] and Jeopardy question generation, and we ﬁnd that our models generate responses that are more factual, speciﬁc, and diverse than a BART baseline.
items.why: Reports generation quality gains on question generation and QA tasks.
items.plain: On MS-MARCO and Jeopardy question generation, our models produce answers that are more factual, specific, and varied than a BART baseline.

items.text: Finally, we demonstrate that the non-parametric memory can be replaced to update the models’ knowledge as the world changes.1
items.why: Claims world knowledge can be updated by replacing external memory.
items.plain: We show that the external document index can be replaced to update the model's factual knowledge as world events change.

items.text: On all four open-domain QA tasks, RAG sets a new state of the art (only on the T5-comparable split for TQA).
items.why: Claims new state-of-the-art performance across all tested open-domain QA tasks.
items.plain: RAG sets a new state-of-the-art benchmark on four open-domain question answering tasks.

items.text: Furthermore, RAG can generate correct answers even when the correct answer is not in any retrieved document, achieving 11.8% accuracy in such cases for NQ, where an extractive model would score 0%.
items.why: Presents specific accuracy result when correct answers are missing from retrieved documents.
items.plain: RAG reaches 11.8% accuracy on Natural Questions even when no retrieved document contains the exact answer, whereas extractive models get 0%.

items.text: As shown in Table 2, RAG-Sequence outperforms BART on Open MS-MARCO NLG by 2.6 Bleu points and 2.6 Rouge-L points.
items.why: Reports specific numerical metric gains on the MS-MARCO benchmark.
items.plain: RAG-Sequence beats BART on Open MS-MARCO natural language generation by 2.6 BLEU points and 2.6 ROUGE-L points.

items.text: Evaluators indicated that BART was more factual than RAG in only 7.1% of cases, while RAG was more factual in 42.7% of cases, and both RAG and BART were factual in a further 17% of cases, clearly demonstrating the effectiveness of RAG on the task over a state-of-the-art generation model.
items.why: Gives human evaluation preferences for RAG versus BART on factuality.
items.plain: Human evaluators judged RAG to be more factual than BART in 42.7% of cases, compared to only 7.1% where BART was preferred.

items.text: For 3-way classiﬁcation, RAG scores are within 4.3% of state-of-the-art models, which are complex pipeline systems with domain-speciﬁc architectures and substantial engineering, trained using intermediate retrieval supervision, which RAG does not require.
items.why: Reports performance comparison on 3-way FEVER fact verification.
items.plain: On 3-way claim classification, RAG gets within 4.3% of top specialized pipeline models without needing direct retrieval training signals.

items.text: Table 5 shows that RAG-Sequence’s generations are more diverse than RAG-Token’s, and both are signiﬁcantly more diverse than BART without needing any diversity-promoting decoding.
items.why: States results on output text diversity compared to BART.
items.plain: Both RAG models generate significantly more diverse text than BART without requiring specialized decoding techniques.

items.text: RAG answers 70% correctly using the 2016 index for 2016 world leaders and 68% using the 2018 index for 2018 world leaders.
items.why: Quantifies the effectiveness of hot-swapping memory to update knowledge.
items.plain: Using matching index dates, RAG answers around 70% of world leader queries correctly, but drops to 4%–12% when the index date does not match the query era.

items.text: We showed that our RAG models obtain state of the art results on open-domain QA.
items.why: Reiterates the main headline outcome in the final discussion.
items.plain: Our RAG models reached state-of-the-art results on open-domain question answering.

items.text: The T5 model with the closest number of parameters to our models is T5-large (770M parameters), which achieves a score of 28.9 EM on Natural Questions [52], substantially below the 44.5 that RAG-Sequence achieves, indicating that hybrid parametric/nonparametric models require far fewer trainable parameters for strong open-domain QA performance.
items.why: Shows RAG achieves higher accuracy with far fewer parameters than T5.
items.plain: T5-large has 770 million parameters and gets an Exact Match score of 28.9 on Natural Questions, whereas RAG-Sequence reaches 44.5, showing that combining parametric and non-parametric memory needs far fewer trainable parameters to perform well in open-domain question answering.
